newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-TOTTENHAM LEFT TO PICK UP THE CRUMBS AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-TOTTENHAM LEFT TO PICK UP THE CRUMBS AGAIN.

text.p: Tottenham have an immediate opportunity to avenge their third-round English F.A. Cup defeat at Manchester United when Alex Ferguson's men visit White Hart Lane for a premier league match next Sunday.

But even a convincing victory over the F.A. Cup holders and league champions will do nothing to disguise the fact that, to all intents and purposes, Tottenham's season ended when the referee blew the final whistle on their 2-0 defeat at Old Trafford on Sunday.
All that Tottenham have left to play for -- with four months of the season remaining -- is a chance of finishing high enough to secure a place in Europe next season.

It is a poor ambition for one of the traditional giants of the English game who seem to have sacrificed their style and flair for organisation and workrate under manager Gerry Francis -- and have still got nowhere.

What is even harder to bear for the Tottenham faithful is that arch-rivals Arsenal have invested in "Tottenham-style" players such as Dennis Bergkamp and Patrick Vieira and are high in the table after seemingly ditching their old pragmatic approach under new French coach Arsene Wenger for a more expansive style which had been the hallmark of Tottenham for decades.
But the feeling of under-achievement is nothing new for Tottenham's long-suffering fans who seem to be involved in a season of transition every season.

When Terry Venables joined Tottenham as manager in 1987 he spoke of building a "Liverpool-like dynasty" with a title in three seasons' time. He was gone six years later, without that title, though he did bring the F.A. Cup back to White Hart Lane in 1991.

Chairman Alan Sugar, the man Venables brought in to save Tottenham from bankruptcy in 1991 and who sacked Venables two years later, said earlier this season that Tottenham would be champions in three years' time.

But Sugar, one of the richest men in Britain and Francis, his manager, have failed to sign the top-class players needed for an assault on the title, which Tottenham last won in 1961 when they became the first English club this century to win the Cup and League double.

Although Tottenham recently signed defender John Scales for 2.6 million pounds ($4.4 million) from Liverpool and spent 2.0 million pounds ($3.4 million) on 20-year-old striker Steffen Iversen from Rosenborg, their recent acquisitions have not been in the same class as, for example, Gary Lineker, Paul Gascoigne, Juergen Klinsmann or Ossie Ardiles.
Scales was in the reserves at Liverpool, while Ruel Fox and Andy Sinton were both out of favour at Newcastle and Sheffield Wednesday respectively before moving to White Hart Lane.

Although Tottenham were decimated by illness and injury in the run-up to Sunday's match, the fact that Francis had to play two 19-year-olds -- one making his debut -- against one of the toughest defences in the League, emphasised the lack of a strong pool of players at Tottenham, an absolute necessity for a club bidding for honours.
Listening to Francis, it is easy for a Tottenham fan to be lulled into a false sense of belief.

"We are joint eighth in the premier league, our 6-1 defeat at Bolton in the League Cup and the 7-1 defeat at Newcastle were aberrations, our season is not over, we can finish high enough for a place in Europe," was his message after the Cup defeat.
But the reality is somewhat different. Manchester United and Tottenham have for decades been regarded as the glamour clubs of English soccer.

Tottenham were the first English side to win a European trophy when they lifted the Cup Winners' Cup in 1963. United became England's first European champions with their famous victory over Benfica five years later.
Both have won the double and they are the two most successful clubs in the 126-year history of the F.A. Cup with United having won the trophy nine times and Tottenham eight.

While United could well go on and make it 10 Cup wins this season and even win the double for the third time in four seasons, Sunday's win over Spurs would just be one fairly routine step on the way to greater glory and riches.
But for Tottenham, Sunday's result marked the end of their trophy-hunting for 1996-97.
